title: 'Gateless Barrier, Case 45: Wu-tsu: "Who Is That Other?"'
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The teacher invites participants to let go of automatic reactions and respond mindfully to their surroundings, encouraging them to question their assumptions and look beyond conventional understanding of Buddhism and enlightenment. This koan invites exploration of the nature of reality and the self, suggesting that true understanding can be found by looking within rather than seeking external answers or guidance. By letting go of attachment to specific goals or identities, participants may discover a deeper sense of freedom and awareness.

sentences.text: *Unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met with even a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Good evening everybody.
Good to see you.
Thanks for coming.
I had another little form thought, a Zoom form, that we might try.
You know how we bow when we enter the physical zendo and when we sit down?
What if, once Zoom finishes connecting, you bow in?
Then it's not this kind of popcorn of bow reactions.
You know how in the zendo, if somebody bows to their cushion and they're sitting next to you, you respond?
So I thought, well, next to you, if they bow, you can bow.
You can try it.
And if you didn't notice, you don't need to be staring at the screen.
Just like in the zendo, if you're kind of in it and don't notice that your neighbor sat down, it's not a big deal.
Okay, let's try that and just mark that I've now arrived at the virtual zendo.
From my point of view, John and Valerie would bow, but you have a different view.
So it's really mixed up in a funny way.
So that's one thing.
And as you notice, I thought we'd do the rope chant at the beginning of every time of practice, just do it together, a little more together since we're so separated.
I thought that would be good.
All right, well, time for another koan. 45 out of 48.
If I just live a couple more weeks, I'll make it.
I'll die happy.
It's funny: with this one, I studied and thought about it and thought, oh, man, this is a tricky one.
I was about to write that on the talk prep.
Then I thought, well, they're all tricky ones.
That's not news.
Why is that even interesting?
Or maybe what it is is my perception of the koan story always feels that way when I first meet it.
You probably have that experience if you read these.
It feels tricky.
Like, what?
Or is it this?
Is it that?
Where am I supposed to go with this?
It's not a usual kind of literature.
But it seems to be the kind of literature where you have to just hang out with it, walk with it for a while, explore it.
And then after a while something does seem to reveal itself, especially if you can get out of the framework of "what's the right answer?"
That's not a right-answer kind of thing, right?
It's beyond right and wrong.
So I felt that way about this one this week, this tricky one, I guess.
But the way it revealed itself to me, yet again, was this quality of a hidden treasure hiding in plain sight.
So tonight the featured teacher is Wu Su.
He's been in a number of the Mu Mon Kahn koans.
The most memorable one is where he talks about a buffalo jumping through the window.
Remember that?
I love that image.
In this case, 39, I think.
I didn't write down the number, but that story was: Wu Su said, it's like a buffalo that passes through the lattice window.
Its head, horns, and forelegs all pass through.
Why can't its tail pass through?
It just has that familiar feeling, doesn't it, of almost there.
Do you feel like you're always almost there?
When are we going to get there?
He's also the teacher who explored with us that wild, far-out Chinese fable about the woman named Qian, who fell in love inappropriately as a young woman.
The pressure of her love for her boyfriend, and her desire to be loyal and proper and be there with her family, her father especially, tore her in half.
She split into two.
Remember that?
Really far out, but a wonderful fable.
The part of her that went off with her boyfriend had a great, wild, cool life and everything, but something was wrong.
Something was off the whole time.
This kind of pervasive guilt and dis-ease was with her even as she had babies and they were getting along great.

Eventually she just has to go back home, there to discover the part of her that stayed behind, who had been sick with grief the whole time and needed her to come back so that the one of her that stayed could heal.
So Wu Su is into all kinds of stuff.
Tonight's story is Wu Su again.
And again, it's one of those where the teacher just gives a single question and that's the whole story.
So we are his students.
It's not an ancient thing.
And the students are some imagined monks somewhere else.
We are it.
So Wu Su said,
*Shakyamuni and Maitreya are servants of another.
Tell me, who is that other?*
*Wu Su said, Shakyamuni and Maitreya are servants of another.
Tell me, who is that other?*
So Shakyamuni is the Buddha of our age.
As you know, we just thanked him a few minutes ago.
And Maitreya is the Buddha of the future.
Another translation of this case, which sounds a little simpler, is:
*Wu Su said, The past and future Buddhas are servants of another.
Tell me, who is that?*
We usually think of Buddha as the penultimate, final thing in this tradition, this mythology, this religion.
And it's really hard to get to be a Buddha.
Really, epically hard.
Bodhisattvas have to practice for lifetimes and lifetimes.
They have to be prophesied by another Buddha that they're going to be a Buddha.
That stamp of approval has to show up.
They have to sacrifice so much and work so hard.
It takes many lifetimes.
And then the system is such that even when they get close, they become so sensitive and open and compassionate that they give it up anyway.
They're like, I'm not going to become a Buddha.
There are so many beings here that need help.
I'm a Bodhisattva.
There's also the thing in the cosmology of it all where you can only have one Buddha per age.
So I wonder how they do that.
Is there a Buddha management committee, or Buddha traffic controllers?
What if one of the Bodhisattvas is about to pop off into Buddhahood and there's already a Buddha in that age?
How does it all work, exactly?
But that's this huge thing, Buddhahood.
Epic.
Grand.
And here Wu Su is doing what Zen teachers are constantly doing.
Maybe I could serve better if I was better at doing this kind of thing: urging us to look beyond even that.
To look beyond our ideas, our fixations.
Look beyond the stuff we want.
Look way beyond.
You're aiming your sights way too small.
Just to be a Buddha is not nearly enough.
Because in the story he says the current and future Buddhas are the servants of another.
So there must be something even better than Buddhas, if the Buddhas serve.
Whom the Buddhas are servants of.
But regardless of all that excellent mythology, this is a good daily practice, isn't it?
Not to be so comfortable with your ideas of who you are and what's going on.
That you'll definitely be happy if you get to do this or that, or get that position at work or in the zendo.
We have these cool positions in the zendo just to dangle them in front of you like either a carrot or a stick, depending on your personality.
It's the same thing.
Make you want it or make you fear it, and it actually doesn't matter all that much.
But it's powerful, because we believe it to be.
So go beyond that belief.
Beyond that belief that I'd be happy if I got to be the Dhamma on a Saturday, or some such thing.
We know it's ridiculous when we even say it out loud to ourselves.
But yet it gets caught up in our heart.
I don't want to be that Buddha sitting there ringing that bell.
Wu Su says, no, that Buddha serves somebody else.
That's not even halfway there.
It reminds me of Norman, who in one of my rakasus wrote, "Even Buddha only halfway there."
I think he wrote it to encourage me to let go a little bit.
I didn't get it at the time.
Still kind of puzzling about that.
Even Buddha only halfway there?
What?
No, he's all the way there, Norman.
You're mixed up.
I was actually a little disappointed.
They've got better stuff on their rakasus.
And to be disappointed is part of this.
Disappointment is also the Dhamma.
So if you notice, and you will, because we all will, your conditioning has been sliding you into the idea that there's something wrong with your disappointment.
You need somebody to fix it, whether it's within the sangha or someone else, it doesn't matter.
Wu Su says, that's not it.
Go beyond that.
Look beyond.
Dogen is constantly saying, study this carefully.
Go beyond.
It's like the six paramitas.
They have the same quality.
Explore this quality: you have an idea of it.
Generosity says, I know how to be nice to people.
I'm a generous person.
Wouldn't you say that about yourself?
And the paramita of generosity says, that's not even halfway there.
There's something beyond that.
Don't be [unclear: "subtle for the ordinary"] generosity, because that's not good enough for the world.
That ordinary generosity divides us as much as it helps anybody.
It makes you a proud giver, and the recipient excited or grouchy or nervous because they don't know if they like this thing you just gave them.
And now they have this obligation to you that they're going to have to navigate.
What if you come over to their house sometime and you didn't hang it up on the wall?
So that ordinary generosity won't do.
Wu Su says, go beyond that too.
Do you remember the six paramitas?
I thought we'd have a quiz.
I'll just hold it on my finger, and you've got to see if you can think of it before I say it, okay?
The first one, I gave it away: generosity.
Second one is ethical practice.
Third one is patience.
Fourth one is energy.
Fifth one is concentration.
And you've got to get the sixth one.
Wisdom.
Yeah.
How'd you do?
Did you get all six?
Fess up.
There are a lot of lists, but that's a good one to know.
It's really worth it, because we're so conditioned that we forget constantly.
So that idea of mindfulness is remembering.
The more we work with them, maybe the more they'll be available when you're next writing a grouchy email or something.
Oh, wait.
This is not generosity beyond generosity, to be griping, complaining.
I wonder if there's another approach.
I wonder if I could find out what's moving me towards that grouchy mood.
Maybe I can breathe with that.
Maybe that's Buddha.
And we can go beyond that too.
So this particular case, though, I'm kind of avoiding the case a little bit.
Who would these Buddhas serve?
Is there an answer to that?
Is there an uber Buddha, a super Buddha?
There are gods, but the gods are a whole different category or something.
And I was going to read you Nyogen Senzaki's commentary, but I see I forgot to bring the book.
So now I have to feel like I screwed up.
But I'll read to you next time.
It's a nice little commentary.
I don't want to remind you about him, because that's another...
It's good to know our ancestors, too.
Know our heart, know our ancestors, know our six paramitas.
And really practice with them all.
So you remember Nyogen Senzaki was an early Japanese priest who came to America with his teacher in the teens, the 19-teens.
And he was such a courageous person.
I'm blown away by this: he stayed behind in America with no job, no plan, almost no English.

And I've been realizing more, because the Awakening to Whiteness anti-racism class I'm taking keeps pointing it out so strongly, and I'm going to try to offer this to us later if it's helpful to anybody, that he was also staying behind in a very racist society.
He was an outsider.
Non-white people were not allowed to immigrate and become citizens until the 50s.
It was written in law.
They challenged it in various ways and it never worked.
Then it worked out that white immigrants could become citizens, but not Asian immigrants, not African immigrants.
I don't know why an African immigrant would have come here then.

So here's Nyogen Senzaki in this foreign land with this dharma that he'd received, with this practice, with this aspiration to be a bodhisattva and help everyone in this strange place have some of this flavor of being able to go beyond their ideas, go beyond their limited views.

The one thing I remember from the commentary I was going to read you, and actually I have a little bit of a quotation here that was like the follow-up after the whole chapter, is that he says that all Zen questions ask for an answer to come from Buddha nature and nothing else.
So your answer needs to come from Buddha nature.
Who are the Buddhists, who are the Buddhist servants of?
The answer to this can only come from your own deepest heart.
It's not from your head, not from your ideas, not from what you read.
It comes from Buddha nature.
And he [unclear: "guides"] Buddha nature as being from the inner being of one's own self, the inner being of one's own self.
And then the next thing he says is, to access this, you must crush the idea of God, which is kind of a hazardous thing to say in a Christian society.
And actually, I think all of us, whether we grew up going to church or not, are Christians, whether we think so or not.
We have some deep mythology in us, and Nyogen Senzaki grew up in a different mythology.

So he encourages students with really harsh language to go beyond that, go beyond whatever framing has happened through biblical and Christian and just consensus understanding, which isn't all of it exactly straight from the Bible or anything.
It's a way of thinking about each other and our world that receives this label of Christian.
The other thing I appreciate about Nyogen Senzaki was just learning a little bit about his weekly routine.
I like to know what people actually did.
So you had a weekly zazen meeting, and you'd sit for 30 minutes in a chair.
And you get a pretty short Dharma talk.
This chapter I want to read to you is only two pages.
It was his Dharma talk in this case.
He didn't talk very long.
And there's some kind of structured question and answer.
I think he would refuse to answer a lot of questions, but some he would comment on.
And then no chitchat.
Everyone left quietly, or he would really scold you.
The Dharma has been delivered, in other words.
And it's time for you to go quietly out of the room and quietly home and see what you really understand.
See if this helps you to shift to a different view, to a view beyond your view.
And that chitchat is just kind of throwing out your concentration, the fifth paramita.
So this is the practice of silence.
And it's funny, when I first read this, it sounded harsh.
Like, oh my gosh.
It would be like putting all these signs in the lobby at the Dharma hall: "No chitchat.
Silent room."
It would take us a while to adjust to that.
I don't know how to channel my inner Japanese master and yell at anybody.
Maybe we would never adapt to it.
Maybe we'd just feel guilty.
And I was thinking about it.
We also get so focused in our own conditioning, right, that we're trying to go beyond.
We're locked into it.
So the people who are just wired to be prone to talk will talk.
The people who are uncomfortable talking in a milling group, getting their shoes on, won't talk, and they'll feel bad.
It's so much easier for a talker to turn the silence into talk, and so much harder for a quiet person to turn the talking into silence, right?
So there's always so much going on.
Every minute that we're alive, especially if we hazard being with other human beings in person or over the Zoom screen, we're adding all these other factors.
And every moment is like a koan, actually, right?
These koans that I was saying are so puzzling are like entering a room with another person.
Really puzzling.
How do we behave together?
How do we act?
What's true for me and you?
What is Buddha, and what is going beyond Buddha?
And how can we answer from this deeper place, the inner being of yourself, from Buddha nature?
Master Muman has a really practical verse in response to this story from Master Wusu.
Master Muman is the author, the collector of these cases.
His verse says: "Don't draw another's bow.
Don't ride another's horse.
Don't discuss faults of others.
Don't explore others' affairs."
Four don'ts.
Don't draw another's bow, like a bow and arrow.
Don't ride another's horse.
Don't discuss another's faults.
Don't explore another's affairs.
So take responsibility, right?
Knock your arrow and draw your own bow, ride your own horse.
Go your own way.
And then we get into some perilous territory for our culture, because we're so separatist and individualist.
It's not exactly what they mean, I don't think.
We go our own way within a context of community, within a context of support.
We need support at this deep fundamental level.
We could never really go our own way.
But when we have what we basically need to function, maybe we could take a little more responsibility and not jump on somebody else's horse, not grab somebody else's bow.
Then these second two lines are just straight-up precepts, right?
We're always studying the precepts around here.
And the reason we're always studying the precepts around here is that we're actually always forgetting the precepts around here.
That's what's happening, right?
So: don't discuss another's faults.
Did you discuss another's faults today?
I fear that I did.
About yesterday, probably.
So I resolve to do better and go beyond that limited way of being, because it doesn't help anybody.
Maybe there's some exploration and I think it's helping, but probably not.
But then Muman takes it even further: don't explore another's affairs.
Don't even get in there.
There's a radical kind of space-giving to that, isn't there?
And a radical kind of trust that the other will be okay without your advice or even your exploration.
Often the exploration is a covert advice-giving, isn't it?
"Oh, don't worry.
I'm not going to give you any advice.
I'm just curious to see what you've got here.
Oh, look at that.
Interesting, right?"
Or "They never mentioned that.
That's the most important thing to me.
Did she just not see it?
Did she not like it?"
So sometimes it sounds exhausting when we try to unpack it.
But the wonderful thing is, the practice also takes care of us at such a deep level.
It's not predictable.
It sure as heck isn't fast.
Someone fed back to me that I said, some time a decade ago, that Zen is a slow cook or a slow simmer.
I had a little experience with that myself today at noon.
I was doing a one-hour little mindfulness teaching online, with my other hat on as the director of Mindfulness Northwest and a mindfulness teacher.
I'm cruising along doing my little lesson, and they seemed to like it fine, just about 15 people.
One of them put something in the chat, which I happened to have open, and I read it, distracted myself for a moment, and came back.
She wrote this so politely.
She said, "Excuse me, maybe if there's time and it might be appropriate, could you mention the Nalanda retreat?"

What the Nalanda retreat is about is this: on Friday, day after tomorrow, Friday evening, 7 to 9, and Saturday together, so a day-and-a-half retreat, Saturday 9 to 4, I'm doing a retreat in collaboration with Nalanda Bodhi, which is one of the biggest Dharma centers in Seattle.
I wrote the title in here somewhere, but I'm having a little trouble focusing on my notes.
I'll find it in a minute.
It's basically on mindfulness practice and Buddhism, how they support each other.
I guess it's something like "modern practice, ancient roots."
Yes, mindfulness: modern practice, ancient roots.
And here I am at noon on a mindfulness call put on by the organization that also sponsored this other event in two days, and it would never occur to me to mention that you might be interested in it.
I don't do self-promotion.
Then I realized, as I was thinking about that while writing the talk: why didn't I mention it to you guys?
You might be really interested, but now it's two days' notice.
So here I've got this funny thing: I just don't think to mention things that I'm going to do that would be really interesting to somebody, or even a group of somebodies, in an obvious way.
The story I've always told myself is, "Oh, it's more responsible for me to keep these two things separate."
It could be really inappropriate for me to spend my whole Dharma talk convincing you to sign up for the mindfulness-based stress reduction class, which costs money and all that.
But this wouldn't be that, right?
It would be worth a minute or two to say, "Hey, next month I'm doing an interesting thing through Nalanda Bodhi.
You might like it.
We can find out a little bit about that world, and we can connect with some Nalanda Bodhi people."
There are going to be people from their sangha and people interested in mindfulness and so on.
But that's what I tell myself: "Oh, I'm keeping these two things separate.
That's appropriate."
Or I tell myself, "Oh, it's just a limit of the way I think.
I keep these two calendars separate, and if I'm in one role, I don't think about the other role.
I just don't think about it."
Sorry.
Oh, well.
But you know what I [unclear: "fleshed"] on during the mindfulness lesson at noon today?
The topic was negative emotions and negative core beliefs, these deep negative beliefs that almost all of us seem to have in there somewhere.
Something around "I'm not good enough," something around shame, something around fear.
They aren't that rational, they aren't reasonable, and they're usually not apparent to us in a conscious way.
But these deep negative beliefs can just run our lives, right?
Sometimes they pop up in such a way that we can trace the thread back and say, "Oh my gosh, look at that."
But other times we're busy, we're distracted, we're not recognizing the way the behaviors look together.
So when this woman in my noon mindfulness session said that, I said, "Oh my goodness, you know what my negative core belief is?
It's a fear of rejection."
It was just so clear to me in that moment.
Who knows what's really true, but I had this clear sense: I don't want to say what I'm doing because you might not think it's cool.
You might not want to go.
And there are layers to this stuff, right?
Even if you did want to go, probably nobody else wants to go.
You might want to cancel by the time it happens.
It might be really inconvenient for you.
I got you all excited about this event with me, and then you signed up and gave up something else you wanted to do, and then it got canceled.
You might be mad at me.
The mind is so tricky.
So tricky, right?
But here's the thing.
I've been doing this for decades, and today, at 12:45 p.m., I recognized it.
I don't know the pattern or the pace of these things, but it's putting ourselves in situations of practice.
It's doing our daily practice.
It's becoming more sensitive to our feelings, and especially, I think, the feelings in the body.
I think we need to really renew our intention that Zen is not a head thing.
It's an embodied practice.
I could feel this tightening in my gut when I said that.
It gave it even more the ring of truth: I'm afraid of rejection.
Sorry.
Would you like to come?
Really?
And then it's not like it's going to change the pattern overnight, but it gives me a little more space, a little more ease around it, and a little more forgiveness, right?
Okay, that's being driven by something really powerful.
It's not just that I'm neglectful, or don't like you, or forget to tell you about these cool things you might be interested in.
I don't know if you're interested, but you might be.
It's relevant to what we're doing, so I should tell you.
And I don't need you to take care of me and instantly drop your weekend plans and come to Nalanda Bodhi.
It's actually not there.
It's on Zoom too, right?
Just a different room.
But I think the important thing is: what are these patterns for you?
There's their manifestation, but then there's something beneath.
So when there's suffering, when there's a manifestation, when there's attention, when, and it can be a pretty mild thing, like a little bit of embarrassment.
That's the most I usually would think about this particular pattern.
I'd be at the Zendo doing a super cool thing that everyone might like, and I realize, as I'm getting on my bike to go home: "Oh, I forgot about the thing, dang it."
It makes me a little embarrassed, right?
It wasn't rocking my universe.
I wasn't ashamed and crying for the rest of the night.
But it is a thread.
It's a moment of discomfort, a moment of unhappiness, a moment of regret.
So our way is to actually take these seriously.
Not get too freaked out about them, but see that as something interesting, something valuable, something for practice.
Because practice is about suffering and the end of suffering.
It's not about getting what we want.
When there's a moment of suffering, be curious about it: what is that about?
Wow.
It's not always a conscious thing, like I never figured it out, right?
But keep practicing and stay curious, and maybe one day the treasure that was hiding in plain sight is revealed.
Could be a dark treasure.
Wusu said, "Shakyamuni and Maitreya are servants of another.
Tell me, who is that other?"
Who is that other?
Who are these Buddhas the servants of?
Maybe we could answer.
Maybe we could be courageous and answer.
All of us, right?
They're servants of all of us, and we are servants of them.
Let's all be wise servants of each other, and servants of the heart.
So in a way it's a trick question, because there is no other, right?
How could there be an other?
Buddhas don't have the capacity for otherness.
They're bigger than that, right?
We all make better choices, I think, when we're in touch with this stuff, don't you think?
So it's really worth some attention.
It's really worth slowing down, right?
There's so much evidence in all of our experience.
Slow down a little bit and don't rush around so much.
Even if you're at home doing nothing, there's an internal way you start rushing around, right?
So keep up your daily practice, all of our daily practices, excuse me, our daily practice, and keep that curiosity humming: what's that about?
Wow!
Aren't I complicated?
And I can change.
Because everything changes.
Here's a few lines from Kabir, version Mystic, I think more or less Rumi, a little later than Rumi, I think.
At least it's some rough translation of something he probably said in some long epic poem.
But here it is, regardless of where it came from.
*Don't go outside your house to see flowers, my friend.
Don't bother with that excursion.
Inside your body, there are flowers.
One flower has a thousand petals.
One flower has a thousand petals that will do for a place to sit.
And sitting there, you'll have a glimpse of beauty inside the body and out of it, before gardens and after gardens.*
*Don't go outside your house to see flowers, my friend.
Don't bother with that excursion.
Inside your body, there are flowers.
One flower has a thousand petals that will do for a place to sit.
Sitting there, you'll have a glimpse of beauty inside the body and out of it, before gardens and after gardens.*
So can you feel that?
Can you feel the flower inside your body that you can sit in and with?
It'll be beautiful, huh?
I have a flower seat.
It'll be a strong flower, I guess.
So thank you for listening to my talk on Mumenkan, case 45.
Minus a little piece, but apparently there wouldn't have been time for it anyway, so that all works out.
If you want to get that book, it's called *Eloquent Silence*.
I don't know if it's still in print, but there's a paperback edition.
It's not too expensive.
It's talks and writings and poems and little photographs and postcards and stuff from Yogen Sunzaki's life, mostly in LA, from the teens to the...
I think he lived until about 1970-something.
So, what are your thoughts?
Oh, announcement.
Just a reminder before we get to that part, because I'd probably forget.
I don't forget about art events, at least, sometimes.
So Saturday, we're hoping the air quality should improve at least a reasonable amount, and it's our only opportunity to do it for various reasons, so we're going to go ahead on Saturday evening at 5.
There'll be a ceremony happening inside and in front of the Dharma Hall, and then we'll do a [unclear: "session"] up the hill to Tina Cummings' store room.
That was just there.
Very nice store room.
Our stuff fits in very handily.
We'll deposit our altar there and do a little final bow and let go of our place.
So Saturday at 5, and you just show up and it'll somehow become clear what to do.
We're figuring it out.
I'll do that on mute.
Any thoughts about all that, going beyond your ideas and negative core beliefs that run you around?
And does this wild mythology inspire you or help you?
Or is it just an expedient means to do that kind of stuff?

verbatim.text: Unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met with even a hundred thousand million kalpas. Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words. Good evening everybody. Good to see you. Thanks for coming. I had another little form thought, a zoom form, that we might try. And that is, you know, like how we bow and we enter the physical zendo and when we sit down and stuff. So what if once the zoom finishes connecting, you bow in, and then so it's not this kind of popcorn of bow reactions. You know how in the zendo, if somebody bows to their cushion and they're sitting next to you, you respond? So I thought, well, you know, next to you.

If they bow, you can bow. You can try it. And if you didn't notice, you don't need to be staring at the screen. Just like in the zendo, if you're kind of in it and don't notice that your neighbor sat down, it's not a big deal. Okay, let's try that and just kind of mark that I've now arrived at the virtual zendo. You know, from my point of view, John and Valerie would bow, but you have a different view. So it's kind of like really mixed up in a funny way. So that's one thing. And then if you know, as you notice, I thought we'd do the rope chant at the beginning of every time of practice.
